1.pericope_label: My breath is corrupt, my days are extinct, the graves are ready for me: are there not mockers with me?

schools.summary: Henry notices that the man has stopped counting in years, the long journey of an earlier chapter having already begun, and reads the going breath and the extinguished days as two figures of one thing, a candle wasting from the moment it is lit; on the graves he asks whether one would not serve and answers from the sepulchres of the fathers, hearing in the plural not only an expectation of death but a desire for it.

Gill takes the corrupt breath medically, as an ill smell that made the man strange to his wife, notes that the Hebrew word carries pain even to the pains of travail, allows the alternatives of spirit and of mind, and rules out the obvious mockers, those who make a mock at sin, in favour of the friends, by whom this man thought himself mocked.

Clarke prefers my spirit is oppressed and collects manuscripts reading made weak or worn down, reads the second noun as sepulchral cells with a probable reference to niched cemeteries, and finds the mockers clause so uncertain that he simply lists the renderings and remarks that the reader has translations enough; Wesley repeats the point about the fathers’ sepulchres and the bed soon made, and puts the mockers clause as the question it is.

Ellicott says the corrupt breath is what happens in elephantiasis, treats the plural graves as Hebrew idiom standing for a singular as the word for blood does, and renders the second clause as a bitter reproach in which the eye has nothing else to look upon; Delitzsch defends the chapter division against those who would move it and refuses the rendering my spirit is destroyed, since the verb means corrupted or troubled and the subject is the breath, grown short and offensive.

debates.question: What is corrupt, the breath or the spirit?

sides.position: the breath, grown short and offensive, announcing suffocation and decay as no longer far off; the verb means corrupted or troubled, not destroyed
the spirit is oppressed, or on some manuscripts made weak or worn down, the Latin giving exhausted
the breath, with an ill smell, drawn with pain; but my spirit and my mind are both possible
the breath, as in elephantiasis, though my spirit is consumed is also read
they are the sepulchres of the fathers, graves in consort, the congregation of the dead to which he must be gathered
Hebrew idiom, the plural standing for the singular as with the word for blood: the sense is simply the grave is my portion
sepulchral cells, with a probable reference to cemeteries where several niches each held a corpse

outliers: Clarke alone gives up on the second verse and prints five renderings of it, from the Latin and Greek versions to Calmet and Coverdale, before concluding that the general meaning is plain and the reader has translations enough.
Henry alone turns the extinguished days into a rule about redeeming the time, since a candle wasting from its lighting may also be quenched by a thousand accidents.
themes: a man who has stopped counting in years
breath standing at the door it entered by
a bed soon made
friends heard as mockers

3.pericope_label: Lay down now, put me in a surety with thee: who is he that will strike hands with me?

schools.summary: Ellicott reads the request as a demand for a present pledge of a vindication already believed in, matches it to Hezekiah’s prayer undertake for me, argues that the surety must be divine if the witness is in the heavens, and remarks how the language fits what has since been learnt of the persons in the Godhead; on the verse about flattery he calls the three Hebrew words most obscure from their very brevity and reports two attempts at sense.

Gill reads the opening word as asking God to put his heart and mind to the case and admit someone to plead it, takes the hidden hearts to be the friends’ and sets the hiding among God’s other acts of the kind, including the hiding of his own providences from Asaph and Jeremiah and Habakkuk, and identifies two specific flatteries in what the friends had said.

Clarke turns the request outward as a challenge to the friends to stake their conduct and their souls on the issue, refuses to let the verb about hiding be pressed beyond permission, and notes that the clause about not exalting them was fulfilled exactly, since all three were condemned and not restored until the man they accused interceded for them; Wesley takes the request as a humble desire that God be surety or appoint one, and draws the inference that a wiser judge is needed.

debates.question: Who is asked to give the pledge, and to whom?

sides.position: God is asked to be surety for him with himself, since a witness in the heavens requires a divine surety, the witness of God to God
God is asked to put his mind to the case and to admit or appoint someone to plead it
the friends are challenged to deposit a pledge and stake their conduct and souls against his before God

debates.question: What does he that speaketh flattery to his friends mean?

sides.position: the words are most obscure from their brevity, running literally for a portion he will tell friends; either the friends are denounced for a prey, or a surety would expect them to share the liability
no settled sense: the general moral is that a man who expects much from his friends will be disappointed, and may leave his children looking for bread
a charge with specific content, the promise of prosperity on repentance and the deceitful speaking for God that infers wickedness from affliction

outliers: Ellicott alone argues from this verse that a sense of obligation demanding exact fulfilment or expiation is itself planted by God, so that only God can answer it.
Clarke alone observes that the prediction about the friends not being exalted came true to the letter, since they were condemned and only restored when the man they had accused sacrificed for them.
themes: a pledge asked of the judge
hands struck in a bargain nobody will make
understanding hidden by the one appealed to
three obscure words

6.pericope_label: He hath made me also a byword of the people: yet the righteous shall hold on his way

schools.summary: Gill observes that the name has indeed become a proverb, for poverty and for patience, neither of which is a disgrace, so that something more reproachful must be meant; he has the eye dimmed by excessive weeping, expects the astonishment of upright men at both the afflictions and the unkindness, and describes the holding on as perseverance set against going back, turning aside and standing still.

Clarke reports the proverbs as current in his own day, refuses the received rendering of the tabret clause and would make the man a consuming fire before his friends, reads several of these verses as spoken in foresight of the restoration, and names the book’s use as the text-book of godly men under persecution; Wesley locates the astonishment in judgments that fall on innocent men while the worst prosper, and has the innocent answer by opposing the hypocrites who make such providences an objection to religion.

Ellicott makes the tabret a signal of warning and compresses the sequence into its logic, the warning astonishing the upright, encouraging the innocent and making the righteous wax bold; Delitzsch settles the disputed noun etymologically, dismissing the derivation from the valley of the Moloch sacrifices and deriving it from a verb meaning to spit out, confirmed by Ethiopic and Coptic and by an Arabic verb meaning to treat with contempt.

debates.question: What does the second clause of the byword verse say?

sides.position: not a tabret at all: reading one pronoun differently, he becomes a furnace or consuming fire before his friends, who will have little reason to mock at the end
a tabret or drum openly, that is, a signal of warning, his case being fraught with warning for others — though some render it an open abhorrence, one in whose face they spit
the noun comes from a verb meaning to spit out, not from the place of the Moloch sacrifices, so the fire of hell is a mistake of the older expositors

debates.question: What does the astonishment of upright men accomplish?

sides.position: it is simple amazement, lasting into later ages, at afflictions laid on so good a man and at the censures cast on him
it is answered by zeal, the innocent opposing the hypocrites who make such providences an objection to religion
it is part of a prophesied use: once the whole history is known, nobody will be stumbled at seeing a godly man oppressed, and the righteous will gain strength by every blast of adversity
the warning astonishes the upright, encourages the innocent and makes the righteous persevere and wax bold

outliers: Clarke alone names one grand use of the whole book, that it casts light on seemingly partial displays of providence and has always been the text-book of godly men under persecution.
Delitzsch alone traces the disputed word through two passages in the Talmud, Ethiopic and Coptic, and the onomatopoeia of the Greek and Latin words for spitting.
themes: a name that became a proverb
a drum beaten as a warning
nothing left but skin and bone
a way held on to rather than found

10.pericope_label: But as for you all, do ye return and come now: my days are past, my purposes are broken off

schools.summary: Gill offers three readings of the summons, a challenge to continue the dispute, a call to repent of their hard speeches, or an invitation to sit and listen, is careful that no day actually passed the bound God sets, and turns the man’s reckoning of his own days into evidence that friends who promise long life on repentance have no wisdom in them.

Henry makes the friends’ comfort itself the folly, since comfort fetched from the possibility of recovery in this world fails when the recovery does, and lists the broken purposes, border and stock and children and the pious designs besides, before drawing the rule that the period of our days is the period of all our contrivances for this world though not of a purpose that cleaves to the Lord; on the changed night he counts a double loss, the repose of the night and the entertainment of the day.

Clarke takes the summons as a dismissal to men too full of self-importance to profit by what they see, calls the verse about past days a relapse into the former gloom and notes how such transitions mark the struggle of piety against gloomy providences, and renders the last clause as light lying too close to darkness to be severed from it, a fine picture of a mind generally dark with occasional gleams of hope; Wesley reads the summons as consent to a debate the friends are resolved on and the changed night as thoughts that will not stop.

Ellicott hears irony in the summons and sharpens the grammar to match, not I cannot find a wise man among you but I shall not find one if you renew the argument, and gives the clause about light to the friends, who so little entered into the case that they wanted the man to believe his night of trial was the reverse of darkness.

debates.question: In what tone are the friends told to return?

sides.position: as a challenge, or a call to repent, or an invitation to listen — all three are possible
as a dismissal: consider your ways and go back to school until you acquire humility and knowledge
with irony, and the following clause should read and I shall not find a wise man, if you do renew the argument
as consent to a debate the friends are plainly resolved on

debates.question: Who changes the night into day?

sides.position: the friends, who wanted him to believe his night of trial was the reverse of darkness and that light was at hand
his own broken thoughts, which cost him the repose of the night and the comfort of the day together
either the friends or the thoughts, which comes to one thing; and on another reading the friends put day before night, against the order of nature

outliers: Henry alone draws a thanksgiving out of the verse, that health and ease which let us welcome the evening shadows and the morning light equally are worth being grateful for.
Clarke alone reads the light that is near as light too close to darkness to be separated from it, and calls the clause a fine picture of a mind with occasional gleams of hope.
themes: comfort built on a recovery that may not come
purposes buried with the days that held them
a night as wearisome as the day
wisdom looked for and not found

13.pericope_label: If I wait, the grave is mine house: where is now my hope? They shall go down to the bars of the pit

schools.summary: Gill will not let the conditional be read as doubt about waiting on God, and aims it at the friends’ offer of a peaceable tabernacle; he rules out two other corruptions before fixing on what the body turns to in the grave, reads the kinship through the household the figure borrows, distinguishes the grace of hope and the object laid up in heaven from the hope of restored prosperity that had no foundation left, and sends man and friends and proffered hopes down together to be barred up.

Clarke makes the reckoning indifferent to length of days, offers his own rendering of the address to the ditch and the worm, takes the word for bars as branches or claws so that it may personify the grave or name the alleys of a catacomb, and explains the gloom historically, since deep shades hung in those times over the state of man after death; Wesley turns the expectation into a discipline of conscience and resurrection hope, hears a child’s claim on a parent’s house, and finds the one consolation in good men resting together where they could not agree.

Ellicott calls the closing verse the most difficult in a chapter that is itself among the most difficult, and lays out the problem of agreement: the bars are masculine and the verb feminine plural, hope is feminine singular, the rule about verbs preceding their subjects does not apply since the verb must follow, and the corruption and worm just named are already in the grave rather than going down to it.

debates.question: What goes down to the bars of the pit?

sides.position: the grammar will not say: the bars are masculine and the verb feminine plural, hope is singular, and the only other candidates are already in the grave
all that he has, the word for bars meaning branches or claws, so either the grave is a monster holding bodies in its gripe or these are the alleys of a catacomb
he, his friends and the hopes they pressed on him, barred up together, the hopes never to rise
his hopes, spoken of in the singular a verse earlier and now in the plural, as is usual in the poetical books

debates.question: Which hope is being asked after?

sides.position: not the grace of hope, an anchor sure and steadfast, nor the object laid up in heaven, but the hope of restored prosperity the friends had pressed
the happiness the friends would have him expect, of no use in such circumstances since nobody would live to see it realised

outliers: Wesley alone makes the grave a bed to be prepared, kept easy by a pure conscience, by seeing Christ lying in it and so turning it into a bed of spices, and by looking past it to the resurrection.

Clarke alone explains the uncertainty as historical rather than personal, since the true light was not then come and even the best of the older believers were left in perplexity about the state after death.
themes: a house that is a grave
corruption addressed as a parent
hope asked after and not found
contenders who will rest together
